answer_text:
We need an integer \(z\) such that

\[
(n+1)z \equiv 1 \pmod{n^2}.
\]

Consider the product

\[
(n+1)(1-n).
\]

Expanding,

\[
(n+1)(1-n)=1-n^2.
\]

Since

\[
1-n^2 \equiv 1 \pmod{n^2},
\]

we have

\[
(n+1)(1-n)\equiv 1 \pmod{n^2}.
\]

Therefore,

\[
z \equiv 1-n \pmod{n^2}.
\]

If we want the least positive residue modulo \(n^2\), we add \(n^2\):

\[
z = 1-n+n^2 = n^2-n+1.
\]

Thus the multiplicative inverse is

\[
\boxed{z \equiv 1-n \pmod{n^2}\quad\text{or equivalently}\quad \boxed{z=n^2-n+1}.}
\]
